:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

When an AI answers a question, the interaction is over. When an AI takes an action, the real engineering has only just begun.

A prompt-and-response model is an oracle behind glass: it answers when spoken to, incurs no permanent consequence, and resets its state the moment the session ends. But when you give that intelligence tools, memory, and a delegated goal, it ceases to be an oracle. It becomes an **actor**.

:::

An actor cannot be engineered as a stateless request. An actor lives across time. It reads a file, writes a script, encounters a compiler error, reflects, and tries again. Every decision it makes either moves it closer to task closure or compounds into catastrophic failure. That multi-step, closed-loop arc—the **trajectory**—is the unit of work that sixty years of computer systems infrastructure was never designed to manage.

In *Introduction to Machine Learning Systems*, we optimized the single node: balancing tensor arithmetic against the physical constraints of silicon. In *Scaling Machine Learning Systems*, we scaled models across fleets of accelerators. But in both volumes, the underlying assumption remained the same: a client sends an input, the model generates output tokens, and the system resets.

Volume III confronts what happens when that assumption shatters.

Autonomy demands long horizons, but long horizons destroy reliability. If a model is 98 percent accurate on any individual step, an unverified fifty-step autonomous workflow will fail nearly two-thirds of the time. Systems engineering is the only discipline that arrests that compounding decay. We must learn to manage context not as a bottomless prompt buffer, but as a structured memory hierarchy; to treat tool execution not as text strings, but as isolated, sandboxed system calls; and to build distributed Sagas with deterministic rollbacks when non-deterministic actions fail in the wild.

I write these chapters as a student of a discipline in motion. Putting this book together is my own way—as an educator and researcher—of wrestling with where the field is heading, sifting through the daily noise of transient frameworks, and boiling down the durable first principles of **Horizon, State, and Authority** that will still govern computing a decade from now.

The field is actively discovering its own foundations. Consider this book an invitation to explore that frontier together.
